_comment: 96 幅画作的英文简释。按用户选择「以英文重写同等信息量」撰写：不逐字直译，但保留原有的学术判断与信息点。titleEn 沿用 manifest 中已有的通行英文画名，不重写。
a01: Bison and signs share the rock face in what is already a ritual image: art here carries memory, hunting magic and collective identity at once.
a02: Aegean palace frescoes record sea life in flowing line and bright fields of colour, revealing the untroubled gaze a Bronze Age trading society cast on nature and the body.
a03: A continuous frieze in a Pompeian villa stages the Dionysiac mysteries as theatre, showing how Roman domestic painting manufactured atmosphere, status and sacred experience.
a04: The mosaics of San Vitale in Ravenna set emperor and church side by side on gold ground and flattened figures; the image becomes a visual declaration of Byzantine theocratic order.
a05: Robed in purple and holding the chalice, Theodora is folded into a sacred order by eternal gold, shaping the public image of a woman ruler.
a06: The Duke of Berry's book of hours sets farming, aristocratic castle and calendar side by side, where late Gothic observation of nature meets minute narrative.
e01: Giotto gave the saints weight, volume and real grief; the Arena Chapel frescoes thus brought human dignity into sacred narrative.
e02: Convex mirror, chandelier and meticulous clothing turn a marriage into verifiable witness; Van Eyck's oil technique marks the summit of Northern naturalism.
e03: Humanism summoned ancient myth again; Botticelli's flowing line brings beauty ashore from the shell, shaping the Renaissance's emotional image of the classical past.
e04: Soft light and pure architecture place the miracle at everyday scale; Angelico's humble, luminous colour gives faith a visible harmony.
e05: Adam and Eve are no longer formulaic icons but flesh enduring shame and grief; Masaccio opens the Renaissance measure of humanity through light and volume.
e06: Geometric order and perspective make a sacred event appear eternal and clear; Piero presents the Renaissance faith in reason with almost musical balance.
h01: Sfumato dissolves contour into air and shadow; Mona Lisa's smile becomes the most enduring pictorial puzzle of modern individual consciousness.
h02: Leonardo compresses the instant of betrayal into a psychological ensemble, perspective converging at the centre, so that narrative, science and drama hold at once.
h03: Plato and Aristotle debate within a grand architecture; Raphael casts classical philosophy and Renaissance humanism into ideal order.
h04: The almost-touching gap between two fingers becomes the suspended instant of cosmic origin; the Sistine ceiling raises anatomy to a double proof, theological and philosophical.
h05: Titian moves the classical goddess into a Venetian noble bedroom; warm colour, silk and body together define a model of worldly desire and painterly sensuality.
h06: Dürer gazes at the viewer in a composition close to a frontal Christ; for the first time a Northern painter raises his own position to that of near-divine creator.
h07: Figures, lightning and landscape form a lyrical scene resistant to simple reading; Giorgione frees painting from text into self-sufficient poetry.
b01: Light enters the tax collector's room from the right like a pointing finger; Caravaggio places divine calling inside dim everyday life, rebuilding religious imagery through darkness and truth.
b02: Blood, wrinkles and spatter at the instant of decapitation are lit with unbearable clarity; Baroque art summons intense spiritual feeling through the truth of bodily violence.
b03: Rubens turns ancient myth into a tactile feast of full flesh, satin and trees; Baroque movement keeps spreading across the surface.
b04: Rembrandt turns a civic militia portrait into an action theatre in progress; the interplay of light, shadow and movement gives collective portraiture epic scale.
b05: The turned glance, pearly highlight and dark ground make an ordinary girl an eternal gaze; Vermeer paints an instant of the mind with optical calm.
b06: Painter, princess, mirrored king and viewer all watch one another; Velázquez makes painting, power and looking itself the true subject.
b07: A woman's arms exert real force, muscles taut; Gentileschi rewrites heroic narrative from lived experience, in one of the most physical images of the Baroque.
r01: Watteau invents the fête galante: aristocratic couples set out for the island of love through a dreamlike garden, Rococo elegance masking time's passing.
r02: A flying pink skirt, a lover in shadow and glances through the shrubs form a flirtatious game; Rococo sensory pleasure reaches its height.
r03: Blue satin and flowing brushwork lift portraiture beyond a record of identity; Gainsborough raises the English aristocratic portrait to lyrical art.
r04: Roman oath, columns and decisive light turn civic sacrifice into an Enlightenment moral lesson; Neoclassicism supplies the revolutionary age with a visual programme.
r05: Socrates drinks the hemlock calmly in prison; David erects a monument to reason and principle through the death of an ancient philosopher.
r06: The painter depicts the French queen in light dress and natural pose; the portrait moves between court protocol and personal charm, and stands as testimony to a woman artist's professional identity.
r07: Goya paints the royal family with near-ruthless realism, ordinary and fragile beneath sumptuous dress, heralding a new critical phase in court portraiture.
m01: Shipwreck survivors struggle and scan the horizon on a raft; Géricault turns a contemporary political scandal into a tragic monument, and Romanticism moves the public with a scene from history.
m02: Liberty bears the flag over the barricade; Delacroix fuses revolutionary energy, allegorical figure and specific individuals into a national symbol.
m03: An Eastern tyrant gazes upon the chaos he has ordered; Delacroix presents the Romantic fascination with extremity through burning colour and piled bodies.
m04: Sunset, steam and an old warship sink into history together; Turner lets the industrial age and a heroic past take leave of each other in light and colour.
m05: A train hurtles out of rain and mist; Turner paints speed, air and the vibration of light as Romanticism's premonition of modernity.
m06: A traveller stands with his back to us above mountains and clouds; Friedrich places the individual soul and the sublime in nature within one boundless landscape.
m07: Clouds, water and a country cart make a tranquil English pastoral; Constable's patient observation of nature won the sympathy of the Romantic age.
s01: A village funeral is painted at the scale of history painting; Courbet refuses lofty subject matter and gives the death and ritual of ordinary people to public scrutiny.
s02: Three peasant women stoop to glean in a harvested field; Millet gives labour dignity and silence through monumental composition.
s03: At dusk farmers set down their tools to pray; Millet paints a rural hour of devotion as the spiritual echo of modern life.
s04: A courtesan meets the viewer's gaze without apology; Manet challenges academic tradition through flat colour and modern subject, and is counted among the beginnings of modern painting.
s05: A barmaid, a mirrored crowd and bottles of drink compose one instant of city nightlife; Manet interrogates modern seeing itself through an unsettled mirror relation.
s06: Silvery trees and water lend landscape a lyrical memory; Corot links classical landscape to the plein-air realism that followed.
i01: Morning mist, an orange sun and reflections in Le Havre harbour are left on canvas in quick strokes; the title gave the Impressionists their name.
i02: Monet returned repeatedly to his Giverny pond in later life; water, reflection and light approach abstraction and become a bridge from Impressionism to modern painting.
i03: The same Gothic facade appears in different colour at different hours; Monet proves that the subject of painting can be light itself.
i04: Sunlight falls through leaves onto dancers and tables; Renoir records a moment of Parisian popular pleasure in warm colour.
i05: Friends, glasses, fruit and the Seine crowd a balcony; Renoir brings Impressionist sociability to its peak.
i06: Degas observes a ballet rehearsal through a tilted frame and an incidental viewpoint; the modern urban body appears between strict training and everyday ease.
i07: Streetlamps, carriages and pedestrians become leaping points of colour; Pissarro draws the rhythm of the modern city into Impressionist experiments in light.
p01: Swirling nebulae, a bright moon and a sleeping village form an inner cosmos; Van Gogh makes landscape the site of a trembling soul.
p02: Thick paint raises sunflower petals like flames; Van Gogh expresses vital energy directly through colour and touch.
p03: Cézanne breaks mountain, trees and houses into a structure of answering colour planes, later seen as a crucial step toward Cubism.
p04: Gauguin completed a great allegory of life in Tahiti; decorative colour and primal figures together ask after existence, origin and destination.
p05: Seurat fixes Parisian day-trippers into a still rite through scientific pointillism, turning the Impressionist instant into structured modern order.
p06: A wavy sky and a screaming figure externalise anxiety as visual sound; Munch makes psychological states a central subject of modern art.
p07: Gold ornament, mosaic-like pattern and an embracing couple interweave; Klimt reshapes love and eternity in the decorative language of the Vienna Secession.
v01: Five dancers join hands in a red ring; Matisse returns painting to the purest rhythm of life through flat colour and simplified form.
v02: Colour, line and form collide on the canvas like music; Kandinsky raises abstract painting to a visual symphony of the inner spirit.
v03: Black lines, primary colours and white ground form absolute balance; Mondrian reduces the world to a universal geometric order through Neoplasticism.
v04: A black square floats on white; Malevich declares that painting can leave object and narrative behind, becoming the zero point of Suprematism.
v05: Circles, geometric facets and colour assemble a half-human, half-mask face; Klee keeps childlike intuition and humour inside rational construction.
v06: A blue horse's curving outline and red hills breathe together; Marc seeks the spiritual essence of animal and nature through unnatural colour.
v07: Sharp angles, diagonals and glaring colour make the modern city a theatre of desire; Kirchner records the vertigo and loneliness of Berlin streets through Expressionism.
x01: Horses, workers and buildings diffuse into continuous energy in the light; Futurism paints speed, labour and urban life as dynamic force.
x02: Elongated body and warm contour fill the modern nude with intimacy; Modigliani turns the line of the School of Paris into elegant silence.
x03: Gaunt form, bare shoulder and fixed gaze are charged with tension; Schiele explores body, psyche and intimacy through nervous line.
x04: Figures are violently compressed and wrenched in a distorted interior; Beckmann presents the trauma and alienation of modern society in a postwar image.
x05: Mechanical lines and bird forms seem to emit an inaudible twittering; Klee dismantles the vitality of a technological age through precise absurdity.
x06: Geometric forms float in pale space; Malevich gives abstract shape a cosmic weightlessness and self-sufficient order.
u01: A farmer and his daughter stand before a Gothic wooden house; Grant Wood shapes the sturdiness and contradiction of the American rural myth in precise realism.
u02: A large golden figure 5 flashes repeatedly against red and black; Demuth fuses Precisionism and urban speed into a visual poem.
u03: Military insignia, numbers and colour blocks assemble an abstract memorial; Hartley hides personal mourning and the memory of the First World War inside military signs.
u04: Winding shapes and natural colour fields abstract the rhythm of lakeshore and fishing rod; Dove proves American abstraction can grow from the experience of land rather than European theory.
u05: Skyscrapers, bridges and waterfront are broken into vibrating lines and colour planes; Marin answers New York's vertical anxiety with the energy of watercolour.
u06: Cables, arches and lights become radiating geometry; Stella paints the modern bridge as a Gothic cathedral of American industrial civilisation.
u07: Transparent colour planes and spires overlap into a prism of light; Feininger fuses Gothic structure, Cubism and lyrical abstraction into an architecture of modern light.
a07: Roman mosaic records the clash of Alexander the Great and Darius III through dense action, oblique perspective and a dramatic instant, embodying the public commemorative function of ancient narrative imagery.
a08: The embroidered strip turns the Norman Conquest into continuous narrative; linear figures, inscriptions and patterned borders form a medieval visual history.
e07: Uccello organises battle through geometric armour, lances and a gridded ground, converting spatial perspective into almost abstract rhythm — a major early Renaissance experiment in order and observation.
e08: Jan van Eyck renders jewel-like detail in oil, gathering redemption, pilgrimage and the observation of nature into a vast altarpiece system.
h08: Michelangelo sets the Holy Family in a circular composition, showing the High Renaissance pursuit of sculptural presence and overall order through twisting bodies, modelled volume and warm-cool colour.
b08: Rembrandt turns an anatomy demonstration into collective psychological narrative through spotlight chiaroscuro; gazes, gestures and light together form a classic of Dutch Baroque group portraiture.
r08: Ingres presents Napoleon's authority in a frontal, symmetrical, icon-like composition, layering Roman imperial imagery, court ritual and Neoclassical clarity into political apotheosis.
m08: Goya records the cruelty of war in a night-lit execution, arranging victims, muzzles and horizon into a moral indictment and opening the theme of individual suffering in Romantic history painting.
s07: Courbet paints ordinary labourers' bodies and work at nearly life size, granting a neglected class the solemn scale of traditional history painting — a manifesto of Realism.
s08: Brown places road-menders, labourers, scholars and gentry together in a modern street, questioning labour and public morality through crowded detail.
i08: Manet borrows a classical composition yet breaks convention with contemporary figures and direct flat painting, bringing modern life, the nude tradition and public scandal into the picture and opening a new space of seeing for Impressionism.
p08: Rousseau organises a dream through clear contour, still moonlight and a stage-like space without depth, showing Post-Impressionism's alternative path into subjective imagination and symbolic image.
v08: Duchamp superimposes successive movements in one picture, rewriting pictorial representation through the spatialised problem of time; this 1913 Armory Show installation view records its place in public controversy over modern art.
x07: Chagall organises the picture through fragmented, inverted village memory, setting childhood, fantasy and colour experience side by side — evidence of the expanding subjective psychological space of early twentieth-century painting.
x08: Schiele gazes at himself through tense contour, bare paper and nervous touch; portraiture turns from traditional likeness to a direct writing of the subject's psyche.
u08: Hopper builds an emotional space of American modern life from an isolated house, still tracks and cold light, turning an ordinary building into a symbol of estrangement and silence.
